title: Durandus: God concurs with secondary causes only remotely and mediately
source_text: THESIS I. DURANDUS Vir inter Veteres Scholasticos celebris, censuit & docuit Deum cum causis secundis concurrere remote & mediate solum: nempe quia rebus omnibus propriam naturam & essentiam dedit, & facultatem agendi contulit, ac utramque Virtute sua continuo conservat: ea lege, ut creaturae singulae Virtute semel a Deo indita, & perpetuo conservata, proprios motus deinceps obeant; absque eo quod Deus earum actus & effectus immediate & per se attingat: Unde sequitur Deum actuum creaturae causam tantum remotam esse, solam vero creaturam causam proximam & immediatam.
pass_a_gloss: THESIS I. DURANDUS a Man celebrated among the Old Schoolmen, thought and taught that God concurs with second causes remotely and mediately only: namely because he gave to all things their proper nature and essence, and conferred the faculty of acting, and continually preserves both by his Power; on this condition, that each creature by the Power once put into it by God, and perpetually preserved, should thereafter perform its own motions; without God reaching their acts and effects immediately and by himself: Whence it follows that God is only the remote cause of the acts of the creature, but the creature alone the proximate and immediate cause.
pass_b_english: Durandus, a well-known figure among the older scholastics, held and taught that God concurs with secondary causes only remotely and mediately.

On his account God gave everything its own nature and essence, bestowed the power to act, and keeps both in being by his continual power. He did so on the understanding that each creature, by the power God once placed in it and always sustains, then carries out its own motions, without God touching its acts and effects directly and of himself. It follows that God is only the remote cause of what creatures do, and the creature alone is the proximate and immediate cause.

choices.why: The Schools' term for God's acting together with secondary causes; 'concurrence' keeps it recognizable as the technical term, with 'cooperation' kept for cooperatio.
